        2 A. Raut degradation in early benchmarks is highly correlated with the quantization strat-
egy and backend mismatch (Dynamic/CPU vs. Calibrated Static/GPU) rather
than just architectural design. By implementing a host-side entropy calibration
pipeline, we enable stable, high-performance deployment on a 4GB Jetson Nano,
bypassing memory-bound on-device training constraints. 2 Related Work The landscape of agricultural computer vision is increasingly defined by the ten-
sion between model complexity and edge feasibility. Current research into wheat
disease detection primarily focuses on maximizing Top-1 accuracy on static
datasets, often overlooking the logistical constraints of field deployment [78].
As noted by Mohanty et al., the transition from high-performance laboratory
environments to the field is frequently marred by dataset integrity issues [8[14].
Pervasive contamination in public plant pathology sets—where cross-split leak-
age artificially inflates performance—remains a critical bottleneck that under-
mines the reliability of reported benchmarks. Parallel to data concerns, the evolution of quantization strategies has shifted
from hardware-agnostic dynamic methods to sophisticated post-training quanti-
zation (PTQ) designed to mitigate the sensitivity of modern backbones. While
literature frequently contrasts the simplicity of dynamic quantization with the
stability of calibrated static approaches [2J5], there is a lack of consensus on the
“fragility” of lightweight architectures like MobileNetV3. We hypothesize that
the observed instability may stem from activation-range sensitivity in depthwise-
separable layers and HardSwish operations, where dynamic scaling may inade-
quately capture activation distributions for these components. Furthermore, evaluation of Edge AI systems requires a shift from singular ac-
curacy metrics toward multi-objective efficiency metrics. Standard benchmarks
fail to capture the trade-offs inherent in agricultural robotics, where a high-
accuracy model that consumes excessive RAM or triggers thermal throttling is
practically unusable. We build upon the concept of hardware-aware optimization
to propose the Deployment Efficiency Score (DES), integrating throughput and
predictive power into a unified success criterion suitable for resource-constrained
autonomous systems. 3 Contribution A: Dataset Contamination Audit 3.1 Dataset Composition and 11.6% Leakage Discovery The primary dataset consists of 14,154 images across 15 distinct classes of wheat
health and disease state (e.g., Healthy, Yellow Rust, Tan Spot, Septoria) [6].
Using MD5 hashing for exact duplicates and perceptual hashing (pHash) for
near-duplicates (with a calibrated Hamming distance threshold for similarity
clusters), we identified that 11.6% of the commonly cited wheat dataset samples
were cross-split “twins.” This contamination allows models to achieve inflated

5.3 Diagnostic Analysis of Quantization Failure
The accuracy collapse observed in MobileNetV3-Large (85.5%→ 31.0% on lap-
top; 41.7% on RPi 5) is not uniform across classes. Certain classes such as
septoria (F1: 0.91 → 0.00) and yellow_rust (F1: 0.97 → 0.13) exhibited
near-complete degradation in class discrimination under dynamic quantization
(Fig. 9). This leads us to hypothesize that the depthwise-separable layers in
MobileNetV3-Large may contribute to a highly volatile activation range that
dynamic scaling may inadequately capture, particularly for features representa-
tive of fungal rusts. 12 A. Raut
Fig. 9. Per-class F1-score breakdown showing the non-uniform degradation of

6 Discussion
6.1 Performance Variability Across Hardware
A critical observation in our CPU-based benchmarks (Tables 3 and 4) is the
performance variability across hardware platforms. On both the Raspberry Pi 5
(Cortex-A76) and general-purpose laptop CPUs, INT8 inference was frequently
slower than FP32 for certain architectures such as MobileNetV3-Large and
ConvNeXt-Tiny. This behavior is attributed to runtime overhead and backend
implementation characteristics rather than the quantization process itself. Con-
sequently, on the Raspberry Pi 5, users must consider the hardware’s specific
instruction set (e.g., DotProd extension availability) before committing to a
quantization strategy.
6.2 Memory–Accuracy Trade-off in Modern Backbones

while preserving predictive performance

4.4 Training Protocol
Models were trained for 30 epochs using the AdamW optimizer (LR= 10−4).
We implemented a freeze-then-finetune strategy: the pre-trained backbone was
frozen for the first 5 epochs, allowing the randomly initialized classification head
to converge without distorting pre-trained feature maps. This was followed by
a full unfreeze and a cosine annealing learning rate schedule for the remaining
25 epochs. This approach ensures a smoother convergence path, particularly for
the depthwise-separable layers ofMobileNetV3,which are sensitive to highinitial
learning rates. Quantization Stability in Agricultural Edge AI 7

5.1 Framework-Dependent Stability
Earlier experiments might suggest that MobileNetV3 is architecturally fragile to
quantization. However, our data suggest that quantization strategy and back-
end selection are the primary drivers of stability. Figures 4 and 5 illustrate the
performance stability achieved through calibrated quantization.
Table 1 presents accuracy across frameworks and precisions. The identi-
cal FP32 baseline of 85.53% for ResNet50 and MobileNetV3-Large was ob-
served in the evaluated configuration and may represent coincidental conver-
gence on the specific dataset and training setup. FP16 results demonstrate
near-zero accuracy loss compared to FP32 baselines, maintaining≈85.4% for
ResNet50/MobileNetV3 and 88.4% for ConvNeXt-Tiny, while unlocking sec-
ondary optimization paths on Maxwell-based hardware.

5.2 The Deployment Efficiency Score
To provide a deployment-oriented comparison between models, we define the De-
ployment Efficiency Score (DES), a heuristic combining predictive performance
and throughput (see Eq. 2 and Fig. 6):
DES = Accuracy × ln(FPS + 1) (2) Quantization Stability in Agricultural Edge AI 9
Throughput is logarithmically scaled to reduce the dominance of extremely
high frame rates and to reflect diminishing practical benefits beyond real-time
operating ranges. DES is intended solely as a relative ranking measure among
evaluated deployment configurations and should not be interpreted as a universal
metric. A limitation of DES is that it uses overall accuracy rather than class-
balanced metrics such as macro-F1 and does not incorporate power consumption
or thermal behavior. Future work should investigate more comprehensive deploy-
ment utility measures.

Concept: Selects the request closest to the current head position. Implementation: Sorts requests based on distance from the head. Advantages: Reduces average seek time. Disadvantages: Can cause starvation for far-off requests. 📌 Example:
• Order of servicing → 53 → 65 → 67 → 37 → 14 → 98 → 122 → 124 → 183
• Seek time = 236 cylinders

3. SCAN (Elevator Algorithm)
Concept: The head moves in one direction, serving requests, then reverses.
Implementation: Sorts requests, moves in a defined direction.
Advantages: Fairer than SSTF, avoids starvation.
Disadvantages: Can still have a high seek time if requests are at extremes.

Concept: Similar to SCAN but resets to the beginning after reaching the end.

Disadvantages: Requires more movement than SCAN.

The marked degradation of MobileNetV3-Large (31.04% accuracy) under dy-

Our results suggest that quantization configuration can outweigh architectural

The implementation of class-weighted loss (Section 3.2) was essential in stabi-

7 Limitations
This study has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting
the reported results.
All experiments were conducted using a single publicly available wheat dis-
ease dataset [6]. Although the dataset underwent extensive contamination audit-
ing and deduplication, reliance on a single source limits the diversity of imaging
conditions, acquisition devices, and environmental variation represented during
training.
External validation on independent datasets was not performed. Informal
testing on web-sourced wheat images suggested reasonable qualitative behavior;
however, these observations were not conducted under a controlled evaluation
protocol and therefore cannot be treated as statistically valid evidence of gener-
alization.
The training process employed standard augmentation techniques including
horizontal flipping, rotation, and color jittering. More advanced augmentation
methods such as MixUp, CutMix, RandAugment, or domain adaptation tech-
niques were not explored.
Experiments were conducted using a fixed random seed (42) and a single
training run per model configuration due to computational constraints. Multiple-
seed experiments and confidence interval analysis were not performed; therefore,
observed performance differences should be interpreted as indicative rather than
